bp: This workshop is about a web where AI agents are not just private assistants inside one product, but public actors that can find one another, exchange messages, coordinate work, and take part in economic and social arrangements. The ordinary object is the open web itself: many independent services, organizations, users, and software workers trying to interact without all being owned by one system. The abstract says the Agentic Web is emerging as billions of agents move from isolated models to web-integrated entities. That shift creates a need for foundations before the surface applications can be trusted. A web agent may need to discover another agent, know how to speak to it, decide whether it has a credible identity, and understand what rules govern the interaction. The workshop therefore serves infrastructure research: shared architectures, protocols, standards, reputation, governance, accountability, and large-scale coordination for agents treated as first-class web entities.
wh: The hard part is that web-scale agent interaction mixes engineering problems with trust, incentive, and responsibility problems. It is not enough for two agents to send text to each other. They need interoperable formats, which means their messages and capabilities must be understood across independent systems. They need discovery, which means a requester must find a suitable agent in a large open environment. They need coordination, which means many agents may have to divide work, resolve dependencies, and avoid conflicting actions. Then the nontechnical pressures enter. An agent can claim skill or authority it does not deserve. A reputation signal can be manipulated. Governance rules can favor one platform or leave harmed users without recourse. Accountability becomes difficult when a bad outcome is produced by a chain of agents rather than one visible actor. The abstract’s phrase “billions of AI agents” matters because small informal agreements break when the population becomes large, open, and economically meaningful.
naive: A smart beginner might try to make every agent expose a simple profile page and a chat endpoint. Other agents could search those profiles, send messages, and decide from the reply whether to continue. That solves a tiny part of the problem, but it leaves the deeper web problem untouched. A profile can be incomplete or false. A plain conversation does not prove identity, authority, pricing, permitted actions, or accountability. Another beginner answer is to let a single large platform run the directory and enforce the rules. That may simplify coordination, but it weakens the open-web goal by creating a central gatekeeper. The abstract points instead toward interoperable architectures, protocols, standards, and societal mechanisms because discovery alone does not create trustworthy coordination.
ap: The core idea is to treat the Agentic Web as a public architecture problem, not as a collection of better individual agents. The workshop’s central move is convening research around the shared layers that must exist between agents: how they are represented as web entities, how they discover one another, how they communicate, how standards make independent implementations compatible, and how social and economic mechanisms keep participation sustainable. In concrete terms, it asks builders to design the roads, signs, identity checks, rules, and dispute surfaces before the traffic becomes overwhelming. The abstract also expands the topic beyond technical compatibility. Reputation, governance, accountability, and large-scale coordination are treated as part of the architecture because agents that can act across the web will affect markets, organizations, and users. The contribution is therefore a research forum and agenda: making the foundations visible so future agent systems do not grow as incompatible islands.
mech: The mechanism begins with an agent that has a task requiring something outside its own system. First, it must discover candidates: other agents, services, or web-integrated entities that advertise relevant capabilities. Discovery requires a shared description layer, otherwise one agent’s way of naming a capability may not match another’s way of asking for it. Second, the requester must communicate with a candidate through a protocol. A protocol is a rulebook for messages: what can be asked, what information must be supplied, how errors or refusals appear, and how a multi-step interaction continues. Third, the systems need standards so the same basic interaction can work across many organizations rather than only inside one vendor’s product. Fourth, the requester needs trust signals. Reputation can summarize past behavior; governance can say who sets rules and handles abuse; accountability can identify who is answerable when an interaction causes harm. Fifth, coordination mechanisms matter when many agents participate together. They must decide who does which part, when to wait, when to hand off, and how to avoid incompatible actions. The output of the workshop is not a single model prediction. It is a shared research space for specifying these layers so web agents can operate as recognizable, interoperable participants rather than opaque scripts talking past one another.
math: The mathematical ideas are the ordinary mathematics of open systems: networks, matching, scoring, rules, and incentives. A network view treats each agent as a node, meaning a place on the map, and each discovery or communication relation as a link. This matters because usefulness and risk are not properties of one agent alone; they depend on who can reach whom and how information travels through the links. Matching appears when a task must be paired with a suitable agent or service. The system needs a way to compare fit while respecting limits such as cost, authority, availability, and trust. Reputation is scoring under uncertainty: many imperfect observations are compressed into a signal about likely future behavior, while admitting that the score can lag, be biased, or be gamed. Governance is constraint design, meaning rules that say which actions are allowed, who may change standards, and how disputes are resolved. Economic mechanisms add incentives: agents and their owners need reasons to participate honestly instead of extracting value without return. The central tradeoff is openness versus control. Too much control blocks a web-scale ecosystem; too little control makes discovery, coordination, and accountability unreliable.
dots: This workshop sits directly inside the repo’s LLM agents and tool-use family, where the common pressure is turning language systems from answer generators into actors that select tools, use websites, retrieve evidence, and coordinate work. The workshop zooms out from one agent choosing one tool to the broader question of how many agents can find and trust one another on the open web. It also connects to the network concept in the repo: once agents form a web, influence, reliability, and coordination are properties of links and paths, not isolated programs. It connects to matching because discovery is really a fit problem between a task and a capable agent. It connects to ranking and reputation because open systems need ways to sort candidates when evidence is incomplete. It also touches privacy, security, and governance work because a web-integrated agent can cause real effects, so authority and accountability must be handled before action becomes routine.
ww: The workshop’s approach works as a foundation because it puts the shared failure points in one room. If researchers only improve isolated agents, each system may become more capable while the web around it remains fragmented. One agent may use a private message format, another may use a different identity claim, and a third may expose useful services without any shared reputation or accountability signal. Bringing foundations, architectures, protocols, standards, economics, governance, accountability, and coordination together reflects the actual dependency chain. Discovery without communication standards finds candidates that may not be usable. Communication without reputation permits interaction without trust. Reputation without governance leaves unclear who handles manipulation or harm. Governance without attention to economic incentives may produce rules that participants avoid. The workshop format is appropriate because many of these choices need community agreement, not only a clever implementation. The intuitive reason is the same reason the ordinary web needed shared conventions: independent actors can scale only when the surfaces between them are predictable enough to build on and open enough to join.
po: The payoff is a research venue for shaping the Agentic Web before its basic habits harden. The abstract promises a forum where researchers and practitioners examine interoperable architectures, protocols, standards, reputation, governance, accountability, and coordination. That buys conceptual and practical alignment: builders can compare what must be standardized, what should remain decentralized, and where technical design must account for economic and societal effects. The result is not an evaluated algorithm. It is a shared agenda for making AI agents first-class web entities that can discover, communicate, and coordinate across independent systems.
limits: The abstract describes a workshop and research agenda, so it does not prove that any specific architecture, protocol, standard, or governance design works. It does not name a deployed system, evaluation method, threat model, market design, or accountability procedure. The claims assume that interoperable standards can be created before incompatible private ecosystems dominate, and that technical and societal mechanisms can be designed together rather than patched separately later. Reputation assumes past behavior can meaningfully predict future trust. Governance assumes affected parties can be represented and rules can be enforced. Large-scale coordination may still fail if agents have conflicting goals, false identities, manipulated signals, or incentives that reward extraction over cooperation.
